author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This solution uses **dynamic programming** to find the maximum number of jumps to reach the last element. It initializes a `dp` array where `dp[i]` tracks the max jumps to reach index `i` (initialized to `-1` for unreachable, `0` for the start). Using nested loops, it checks each pair of indices and if the absolute difference between their values is within the `target` range, it updates `dp[j]` to the maximum of its current value or `dp[i] + 1`. This works but processes unreachable indices inefficiently, making it slower than optimized versions.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This is an optimized version of the previous approach that adds a crucial **early-exit optimization**: `if (dp[i] === -1) continue;`. Since `dp[i] === -1` means index `i` is unreachable, skipping it avoids unnecessary inner loop iterations. The rest of the algorithm remains the same—it uses a `dp` array to track maximum jumps to each index, and for each reachable position, it tries to jump to all positions whose value difference is within the `target` range, updating `dp[j]` to the maximum number of jumps. This optimization significantly improves performance.

author: Vitor
aiExplanation: This is the most optimized version, building on the previous approach with an additional condition: `dp[j] <= dp[i]`. This ensures `dp[j]` is only updated when it either hasn't been reached yet (`dp[j] === -1`) or the current path has fewer jumps than any previous path to `j`. By replacing `Math.max()` with a direct assignment, it avoids redundant updates and stops processing once a position has been reached with the fewest possible jumps. Combined with the earlier `if (dp[i] === -1) continue;` check, this creates a highly efficient **dynamic programming solution** that maximizes jumps from each reachable index within the value-difference `target` constraint.
